entries.sentence: A lifelong condition in which the immune system mistakenly attacks nerves in the brain and spinal cord.
entries.note: NHS: lifelong condition affecting brain and spinal cord; MS Society: symptoms caused by immune system attacking nerves in brain or spinal cord by mistake.

entries.sentence: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a lifelong condition that affects the brain and spinal cord.
entries.note: NHS: lifelong condition affecting brain and spinal cord.

entries.sentence: Its symptoms come from the immune system attacking nerves by mistake, and the NHS says it is not known why this happens.
entries.note: NHS: not known why; MS Society: immune system attacks nerves by mistake.

entries.sentence: Symptoms vary widely, can come and go and can change over time.
entries.note: MS Society: symptoms can come and go and change over time; MedlinePlus/NHS list a wide range.

entries.sentence: It is most often diagnosed between the ages of 20 and 40, although it can be seen at any age.
entries.note: Search summary said sources give 20 to 40 as most common diagnosis age; not attributed to a single page. Second pass should confirm.

entries.sentence: There is currently no cure, but treatments can slow the progression of MS and help ease symptoms.
entries.note: NHS: no cure currently, treatments can slow progression and ease symptoms.

entries.sentence: The immune system attacks nerves in the brain or spinal cord by mistake, and the NHS says the reason is not known.
entries.note: NHS: not known why; MS Society: immune system attacking nerves by mistake.

entries.sentence: NINDS describes MS as believed to be an autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks myelin, and without myelin nerve signalling breaks down.
entries.note: NINDS: exact cause unknown, believed autoimmune; attack on myelin; without myelin nerve signalling breaks down.

entries.sentence: Low vitamin D levels and genetic factors are also implicated, according to NINDS.
entries.note: NINDS: low vitamin D and genetic factors also implicated.

entries.sentence: Epstein-Barr virus, which causes infectious mononucleosis, is the virus most consistently linked to the development of MS.
People who smoke are more likely to develop MS and to have a more aggressive disease course.
entries.note: NINDS: smokers more likely to develop MS and have more aggressive course.

entries.sentence: Low vitamin D levels.
Genetic factors.
Areas of scar-like tissue, called lesions or plaques, in the brain and spinal cord, where the immune system has attacked myelin.
entries.note: NINDS: distinctive scar-like areas (plaques or lesions) from immune attack on myelin.

entries.sentence: Temporary worsening of existing symptoms with heat, illness or fatigue, which NICE-linked guidance calls a pseudo-relapse.
entries.note: Search summary of NICE/NHS pages: temporary worsening from heat, illness or fatigue is a pseudo-relapse.

entries.sentence: Worsening symptoms that lead to increased disability over time in some people.
entries.note: NINDS: some experience worsening symptoms leading to increased disability over time.

entries.sentence: Relapses, when new symptoms develop or existing symptoms worsen.
entries.note: NICE: relapse defined as new or worsening symptoms lasting over 24 hours with no infection or other cause.

entries.sentence: Bladder, bowel and sexual problems.
entries.note: NHS lists bladder and sexual problems; NINDS booklet covers bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction.

entries.sentence: There is no single test for MS.
Assessment can include a review of health history and symptoms, a physical and neurological examination, an MRI scan, blood tests to rule out other conditions, and sometimes a lumbar puncture.
entries.note: MedlinePlus summary listing these tools; attributed to MedlinePlus.

entries.sentence: People are referred to a neurologist, and NICE says only a consultant neurologist should make the diagnosis.
entries.note: NHS: referred to neurologist; NICE: only consultant neurologist should diagnose.

entries.sentence: There is currently no cure, but treatments can slow progression and ease symptoms.
Disease-modifying therapies can reduce the number and severity of relapses in some people, and are prescribed to people with relapsing remitting or secondary progressive MS who meet certain criteria.
entries.note: NHS summary: DMTs reduce relapses; only for RRMS or SPMS meeting criteria such as number of relapses.

entries.sentence: Relapses may be treated with steroids, ideally as early as possible.
entries.note: NICE: treatment recommended as early as possible; NINDS: steroids for attacks.

entries.sentence: Symptom management can include muscle relaxants, physiotherapy and cognitive behavioural therapy to help with anxiety, depression and fatigue.
The cause of MS is not known, and the sources reviewed do not describe a proven way to prevent it.
entries.note: NHS: not known why; no prevention advice retrieved. Statement is about absence in sources.

entries.sentence: NINDS reports that people who smoke are more likely to develop MS and to have a more aggressive disease course.
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for sudden weakness or numbness in one arm, loss or blurring of vision, or problems with balance and coordination, which can signal a stroke.
For suspected MS symptoms, the NHS advises seeing a GP, who arranges referral to a neurologist.
entries.note: NHS: see a GP; referred to neurologist.

entries.sentence: MedlinePlus advises contacting a healthcare provider if MS symptoms get worse even with treatment.
entries.note: MedlinePlus: contact provider if symptoms get worse even with treatment.

entries.sentence: The NHS lists many possible symptoms of MS, including fatigue, blurred vision or eye pain, numbness or tingling, and problems with balance and coordination.
Muscle spasms and stiffness, bladder problems, difficulty with memory or concentration, and sexual problems are also listed.
The MS Society says symptoms can come and go and can change over time.
The MS Society describes fatigue as an overwhelming tiredness rather than ordinary tiredness.
It adds that when people are fatigued, their limbs can feel heavy and it can be harder to grasp things or to write.
Numbness and tingling are described as an unusual feeling of prickling, itching or crawling insects under the skin, caused by nerve damage in the brain or spinal cord.
Weakness in the upper body and legs, and limited mobility, are listed among the symptoms of advanced MS.
Having these symptoms does not mean someone has MS, but the NHS says they should be checked.
MedlinePlus notes that many people with MS find symptoms are worse with a fever, with heat, or after common infections.
entries.note: MedlinePlus encyclopedia (attribution to this page inferred from summary).

entries.sentence: The NHS names three main types: relapsing remitting, secondary progressive and primary progressive MS.
According to the NHS, about 85% of people with MS have relapsing remitting MS when it starts.
In relapsing remitting MS, people have relapses followed by periods of recovery, the MS Society explains.
entries.note: MS Society contrast with primary progressive.

entries.sentence: Over time, relapsing remitting MS often develops into secondary progressive MS.
entries.note: Search summary; attribution to a single page not certain.

entries.sentence: Primary progressive MS involves symptoms that steadily worsen without remission, and it is less common than the other types.
entries.note: MS Society: symptoms get steadily worse over a long time; less common wording from search summary.

entries.sentence: NICE says a relapse is diagnosed when new symptoms develop, or existing ones worsen, for more than 24 hours, with no infection or other cause, after a stable period of at least one month.
Heat, illness or fatigue can cause a temporary worsening called a pseudo-relapse, which does not need treating, although any urinary infection is checked for and treated.
NICE adds that relapses should be assessed by a healthcare professional with MS expertise, because not all relapses need steroid treatment.
The NHS says there is no single test for MS and that people are referred to a neurologist.
NICE says only a consultant neurologist should make the diagnosis.
Assessment can include a review of health history and symptoms, a physical and neurological examination, blood tests to rule out other conditions, and sometimes a lumbar puncture.
A published review notes that early diagnosis is difficult because there is no single diagnostic test and many features are shared with other diseases.
entries.note: PMC review: lacks a single diagnostic test and shares clinical features with other diseases.

entries.sentence: An MRI scan can show the scar-like areas, called plaques or lesions, that result from the immune attack on myelin.
entries.note: NINDS describes lesions; MRI visibility from PMC/search summary.

entries.sentence: NINDS says that identifying this damage can allow a full diagnosis of MS even after a single attack.
NICE's committee chose to base diagnosis on the McDonald criteria and stressed excluding fever and infection, which can mimic MS symptoms.
It noted that fatigue, depression and dizziness would not usually suggest MS unless accompanied by neurological symptoms and signs.
The NHS says there is currently no cure for MS, but treatments can slow its progression and help ease symptoms.
Disease-modifying therapies can help reduce the number and severity of relapses in some people.
entries.note: NHS; NINDS: reduce frequency of attacks.

entries.sentence: They are only prescribed to people with relapsing remitting or secondary progressive MS who meet certain criteria, such as the number of relapses they have had.
NICE recommends that treatment for a relapse starts as early as possible, and within 14 days of symptoms beginning.
NINDS lists steroids for attacks, muscle relaxants for stiffness and medicines for fatigue among the ways symptoms are managed.
Symptom management can also include physiotherapy and cognitive behavioural therapy to help with anxiety, depression and fatigue.
NICE's public information says many symptoms can be treated, and that medicines can reduce how often and how severely relapses occur.
The NHS and NICE both describe MS as a lifelong condition.
NICE says it affects approximately 130,000 people in the UK.
NINDS says a small number of people with MS have mild symptoms and little disability.
Others have worsening symptoms that lead to increased disability over time.
The MS Society notes that symptoms can come and go and can change over time, so the picture differs from person to person.
entries.note: MS Society: come and go, change over time; 'differs between people' is a light inference.

entries.sentence: NINDS also states that most people with MS have a normal life expectancy.
The MS Society has information on how temperature affects MS, and calls heat sensitivity Uhthoff's phenomenon.
Weakness is mentioned as one common effect of heat sensitivity.

entries.sentence: Its page on advanced MS lists limited mobility and weakness in the upper body and legs among the symptoms.
The NHS advises seeing a GP for anyone who thinks they have symptoms of MS, and having them checked does not mean the diagnosis is MS.
